Article Title: In 1963, Maurice Hilleman swabbed his 5-year-old daughter’s throat after she caught mumps; four years later, the vaccine built from her virus strain was licensed in the US and remains in use
Article Text:
Jeryl Lynn comforts her crying sister Kirsten during a 1966 vaccination with the Jeryl Lynn Strain.

From Jeryl Lynn’s infection to a vaccine

A mumps quarantine sign dating to sometime after 1909.

Why the mumps vaccine mattered

The virus sample was kept for decades

In 1963, vaccine researcher Dr Maurice Hilleman was working to develop a safe and effective vaccine against mumps when his five-year-old daughter, Jeryl Lynn, developed the disease. One night, Jeryl Lynn woke Hilleman and showed him her swollen cheeks, a characteristic sign of mumps. He then swabbed her throat to collect a sample of the virus and drove it to his laboratory.Hilleman was the chief virologist at Merck Research Laboratories in the 1960s and had set out to create a mumps vaccine. At the time, mumps was considered a common childhood illness, and many parents underestimated its dangers. According to the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, scientists had already tried to develop a vaccine, but earlier attempts had problems. Some vaccines caused too many mumps symptoms, while others did not provide enough immunity.Jeryl Lynn’s infection gave Hilleman a chance to try a different approach. He suspected that he needed to work with another strain of the virus. After collecting the sample from his daughter, he began trying to weaken the virus, a process known as attenuation.The aim was to make the virus weak enough that it would not cause mumps, while still allowing it to produce immunity.Hilleman achieved this by introducing the virus to generations of chicken embryo cells. With each generation, the virus changed. It became better at attacking the chick cells and less able to attack human cells. The resulting vaccine strain was officially named the Jeryl Lynn Strain, after the child whose infection provided the original virus sample.Human testing showed that the Jeryl Lynn Strain vaccine could produce strong immunity without causing the disease in vaccinated children. The work then moved towards clinical use, including a remarkable connection within the Hilleman family.Jeryl Lynn herself could not benefit directly from the vaccine that carried her name. Her younger sister, Kirsten Jeanne Hilleman, did. In 1966, Kirsten was immunised with the investigational vaccine. A photograph from that year shows Jeryl Lynn comforting her younger sister as Kirsten received the vaccine from Dr Robert Weibel.The Smithsonian says the vaccine was developed from the virus collected from Jeryl Lynn’s mumps infection. Its collection also includes vials of the investigational vaccine used to immunise Kirsten.In 1967, the US Food and Drug Administration approved Merck’s mumps vaccine. The vaccine developed by Hilleman remains in use today and is still derived from the Jeryl Lynn strain. The Smithsonian also notes that doctors began administering the Jeryl Lynn Strain mumps vaccine to the American public in early 1968.The vaccine was developed against a disease that could cause more than the familiar swelling of the jaw and cheeks. Most people who contract mumps recover fully, but the disease can also lead to serious and sometimes permanent complications.These include inflammation of the testicles and ovaries, encephalitis, which is swelling of the brain, meningitis, which is infection of the tissue around the brain and spinal cord, seizures and deafness.Before vaccination, mumps was also a significant cause of acquired deafness in childhood in the United States. The Smithsonian noted that the disease was once so common that it was often treated as a normal part of growing up, even though it could have serious consequences.The museum marked 50 years of mumps vaccination in America in 2018. It described how the vaccine helped make the swollen cheeks associated with mumps a thing of the past for many Americans.The change was also reflected in popular culture. The Smithsonian holds two Norman Rockwell prints from around 1972 that were commissioned by Merck Research Laboratories to celebrate vaccination and the changing American experience of childhood disease. One of the works shows a family having to cancel a fishing trip after their son develops mumps.The story of the Jeryl Lynn Strain did not end with the vaccine’s development. The Smithsonian later acquired an object connected to the preservation of the virus stock used for vaccine production.The museum acquired a shiny stainless-steel 15-litre canister that had stored part of the frozen Jeryl Lynn virus “seed stock”. It was one of five canisters used to keep the entire supply safe and pure. According to the Smithsonian, the stock kept in the canister could produce 3.26 billion doses of vaccine.The container had protected the stock for years, but its green neoprene stopper eventually began to fail. That created a problem because the virus stock had to be moved without becoming contaminated or losing its potency.In 2015, Merck scientists undertook the task of thawing and transferring the precious seed stock into new containers. The Smithsonian said that if the stock had lost its potency or become contaminated during the transfer, it could have taken five to seven years to produce new stock.The transfer was successful. The Jeryl Lynn stock was moved into a more secure type of container, while the old stainless-steel canister became part of the Smithsonian’s collection.
Article Summary: The Smithsonian says the vaccine was developed from the virus collected from Jeryl Lynn’s mumps infection. Her younger sister, Kirsten Jeanne Hilleman, was immunised with the investigational vaccine in 1966. The vaccine remains in use today and is still derived from the JerylLynn strain.

Article Title: Crews digging 12 feet below a California infrastructure project uncovered 40- to 45-million-year-old bones of a large hoofed mammal; paleontologists spent seven days extracting the fossil from hardene
Article Text:
A mystery buried beneath modern Oceanside

Scientists have two possible suspects

Seven days beneath tonnes of rock

The find could reveal more about ancient California

A routine infrastructure project in Oceanside, California, has uncovered a glimpse of a world that existed tens of millions of years before humans. The City of Oceanside first announced the discovery on September 22, while reporting from the Los Angeles Times, NBC 7 San Diego and the San Diego Union-Tribune provided additional details about the excavation and the scientists working to identify the animal. The fossilised remains were found about 12 feet beneath the surface during excavation for a city water infrastructure project. Several limb bones, ribs and other fragments were recovered, with the largest bone measuring more than two feet long, according to the Los Angeles Times. What makes the discovery particularly intriguing is that scientists still cannot say exactly what animal the bones belonged to.Paleontologist Joseph El Adli was conducting routine monitoring at the construction site when he spotted what appeared to be bone protruding from the excavation. The discovery prompted the area to be secured and the excavation to shift from ordinary construction work to a careful fossil recovery operation.The fossils were embedded in the Santiago Formation, a sequence of sedimentary rocks found across parts of northwestern San Diego County. The particular section where the remains were found dates to the Eocene Epoch, a period that lasted from about 56 million to 33.9 million years ago.At the time, Southern California looked nothing like it does today. The region was warmer, wetter and heavily vegetated, providing habitat for large herbivorous mammals that have long since disappeared.The fossils have been dated to roughly 40 to 45 million years ago, placing them within the Uintan North American Land Mammal Age.Based on the size and shape of the recovered bones, El Adli has narrowed the possibilities to two extinct groups of odd-toed hoofed mammals.One is the Brontotheriidae, a family commonly associated with animals nicknamed thunder beasts. These large herbivores were related more distantly to today’s horses and rhinoceroses and included species with substantial bodies and distinctive skulls. Some brontotheres developed prominent bony projections on their noses.The other possibility is an amynodont, an extinct group of rhinoceros relatives sometimes described as swamp rhinos. They were generally hornless and had broad, barrel-shaped bodies. Some species are believed to have spent considerable time around water.Both possibilities fit the broad picture provided by the bones, but the researchers need additional anatomical evidence before they can make a more precise identification. The skull, teeth or lower jaw would be particularly valuable because those features can provide clues that isolated limb bones cannot. (NBC San Diego⁠￼)Finding the fossils was only the beginning. Once the bones were spotted, El Adli and his team spent seven days carefully exposing them from several tonnes of hardened mudstone and sandstone.The work was done largely by hand to avoid damaging the fragile material. NBC 7 reported that roughly six feet of rock had to be removed by hand to reach the bones from the excavation where they were first identified. (NBC San Diego⁠￼)After the bones were exposed, they were protected inside a plaster field jacket. This is a standard fossil-recovery technique that allows fragile specimens, along with some of the surrounding rock, to be transported without breaking apart.The fossils have now been moved to an off-site laboratory, where specialists will remove the remaining rock and stabilise the bones with conservation materials.The discovery is also significant because it adds to the growing fossil record of the Santiago Formation. Fossils from the formation have previously revealed that the San Diego region supported very different ecosystems during the Eocene.Researchers hope that further preparation will reveal enough anatomical detail to identify the animal more precisely. If additional bones, teeth or jaw material are found at the site, they could provide even more information about the species and how it lived.For now, the City of Oceanside is keeping the precise discovery site confidential. Officials say the decision is intended to protect both public safety around the active construction area and the fossil locality itself from unauthorised digging.The fossils are ultimately expected to become part of a museum collection, where they can be preserved and made available for scientific research and public viewing.For a project designed to build part of modern Oceanside’s infrastructure, the excavation has unexpectedly opened a window into a much older California, one where enormous hoofed mammals moved through a warm, forested landscape roughly 40 million years ago.
Article Summary: The fossilised remains were found about 12 feet beneath the surface during excavation for a city water infrastructure project in Oceanside, California. Several limb bones, ribs and other fragments were recovered, with the largest bone measuring more than two feet long. The fossils have been dated to roughly 40 to 45 million years ago.

Article Title: In 1971, engineer Godfrey Hounsfield’s new scanner revealed a brain cyst in the first clinical CT scan; 8 years later, he shared the Nobel Prize for developing computer-assisted tomography
Article Text:
Godfrey Hounsfield stands beside the EMI-Scanner in 1972 and modern CT scans provide much higher resolution images of the 'slices' of the brain than Hounsfield's original scan did in 1971.

From radar to an extraordinary idea

Turning the brain into slices

From laboratory experiment to hospital

X-rays beam through each ‘slice’ of brain, oriented at each degree from 1 to 180 in a semicircle

A medical revolution

What if the contents of a sealed box could be revealed without ever opening it? For British engineer Godfrey Hounsfield, the question began with an unlikely fascination with Egyptian pyramids and cosmic rays. Years later, that same idea would lead to a machine capable of looking through the skull and revealing the soft tissue of the human brain. On October 1, 1971, his invention produced the first clinical CT image of a human brain, identifying a cyst that conventional X-rays could not clearly show, states an online report by Smithsonian Magazine.According to the report, Hounsfield's career began far from medicine. During the Second World War, he worked with radar in the Royal Air Force, where his talent for electrical equipment quickly became apparent. After the war, he trained as an engineer and joined EMI, the British electronics company that would later become famous for its association with The Beatles. By the 1960s, Hounsfield had become a leading figure in computing. When EMI withdrew from the computer business, however, he found himself with greater freedom to pursue unconventional ideas.One of them involved seeing inside objects without opening them.His interest in whether cosmic rays could reveal hidden spaces inside pyramids eventually evolved into a medical question after he encountered the limitations of conventional brain X-rays. Bones appeared clearly, but soft brain tissue largely merged into an indistinct mass.Hounsfield's solution was deceptively simple in concept. He imagined dividing the brain into a series of thin slices, like cutting a loaf of bread. X-rays could then be directed through each layer from numerous angles, with detectors recording how much radiation passed through, adds the online report.Different tissues absorb X-rays differently. By collecting thousands of measurements and feeding them into a computer, Hounsfield developed a method to calculate the density of tiny sections within each slice and reconstruct them into an image, the report adds.If we go by the report, the first machines were far from today's sleek scanners. Working with limited resources, Hounsfield assembled an experimental system from equipment and components available around EMI's research facilities. Early tests on objects and animal brains demonstrated that the concept could distinguish structures that ordinary X-rays could not.The biggest obstacle was proving the technology could work safely on people. Hounsfield's project received crucial support from within EMI and eventually from Britain's Department of Health and Social Security, which agreed to purchase scanners for hospitals even before the machines were completed.A full-sized scanner was installed at Atkinson Morley Hospital in London. On October 1, 1971, a woman with suspected brain disease became the first patient to undergo the procedure.The process was painfully slow by modern standards. The scan took about 30 minutes, while the data had to be transported across London on magnetic tapes for processing by an EMI mainframe. Several hours later, an image could finally be produced, explains the online report from 2021. The result was unmistakable: a cystic mass was visible in the patient's frontal lobe, it adds.The breakthrough quickly changed the way doctors investigated disease inside the body. CT imaging made it possible to locate tumours, bleeding and other abnormalities without exploratory surgery.The technology soon expanded beyond the brain. In 1973, American engineer Robert Ledley developed a whole-body CT scanner, opening the door to imaging organs, blood vessels and other structures.Hounsfield shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the development of computer-assisted tomography. He was knighted in 1981 and continued working on inventions until his death in 2004. Today, CT scanners are vastly faster, sharper and more efficient, with substantially lower radiation exposure than early machines. More than 80 million CT scans were being performed annually in the United States by 2020, illustrating just how deeply Hounsfield's idea became embedded in modern medicine.And his original fascination with hidden spaces came full circle. Cosmic-ray detectors have since been used to investigate the pyramids, including the discovery of a previously unknown chamber inside the Great Pyramid of Giza in 2017. The engineer who wanted to see inside a pyramid ultimately gave medicine a way to see inside us.Images Courtesy: Smithsonian Magazine
Article Summary: Godfrey Hounsfield's invention produced the first clinical CT image of a human brain, identifying a cyst that conventional X-rays could not clearly show. He shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the development of computer-assisted tomography. Today, CT scanners are vastly faster, sharper and more efficient.

Article Title: An Atlanta mansion built in 1924 for Thomas Jefferson’s great-great-grandson faced demolition; in 2013, its new owners cut the 8,000-sq-ft home in two and moved it about 2 miles to save it
Article Text:
Built for a Jefferson descendant

Peachtree Road

The sale and trouble

Taking a mansion apart to keep it whole

Some historic homes are preserved by restoring their walls, replacing their old roofs, and repairing the damage. But the Randolph-Lucas-Jones House in Atlanta required something else. It needed a police escort, utility crews to lift power lines out of its path, and a roof hinged down so each half could clear the route. Built in 1924, the 8,000-square-foot mansion was moved about 2 miles in 2013 after its new owners stepped in to save it from demolition, according to the Georgia Trust for Historic Preservation.The Georgian Revival-style home was built in 1924 for Hollins Nicholas Randolph, an Atlanta attorney and businessman and the great-great-grandson of Thomas Jefferson. The house was designed by architect P. Thornton Mayre, who also helped build the Fox Theatre. The home’s design was based on the plan of Randolph’s ancestral home near Charlottesville, Virginia. The Randolphs lived there for about a decade before selling it to Margaret Lucas in 1935. Her husband, Arthur, operated several cinemas around the city, according to Rough Draft Atlanta. She stayed until her death in 1987. The house later became a fixture of fiction, too. A painting of it appeared on the cover of Anne Rivers Siddons’s 1988 bestselling novelIn 1998, the Lucas family sold the property to the 2500 Peachtree Condo Association. During this time, the house was shifted forward on its lot, with plans to use it as a clubhouse and an event space. Maintenance bills quickly ended that idea, and the house fell into disrepair. By the autumn of 2012, the association held a city demolition permit and was offering the house free to anyone who could move it.Roger Smith and his husband, the late preservation advocate Christopher M. Jones, got the news while they were at a function at the Atlanta History Center. City Council member Mary Norwood pulled Jones into a corner for a private conversation. “Mary came up to us and pulled Christopher away into a corner for a private conversation. She told him the house was going to be demolished, and I think he decided that night we had to save it,” Smith told the outlet. Their firm, NewTown Partners, focused on distressed historic properties. Smith and Jones were chosen as project partners in January 2013. They closed on the empty lot at 78 Peachtree Circle in Ansley Park on May 30, which became the house’s new location. They also agreed to donate a preservation façade easement to the Georgia Trust for Historic Preservation, so the exterior could never be torn down. The project reportedly had a $1.5 million budget.To save the mansion, it first had to be carefully dismantled. Preparations began in July, when the crew removed the brick façade and slate roof, significantly reducing the building’s weight. The bricks were carefully set aside to be cleaned and reinstalled after the move. Adjustments were to be made inside: the second-floor doors and baseboards were pulled and numbered so each could return to its original spot. The frame was split above the first floor, and each section topped out at 19 feet.The move began on November 8, 2013. A temporary road was built across a vacant lot opposite the Woodruff Arts Center, giving the trucks a direct run to the new address. The trip was 2.1 miles and took seven hours, according to the Georgia Trust. The house was slowly moved using hydraulic lifts, the trust said.Setting the house down was the easy part. The comprehensive rehabilitation began in 2014. Smith and Jones sold their own home and rented an apartment behind the lot to oversee the work. Smith has described money as a monthly puzzle of what could be paid for and finished. “There was this misnomer that we had all this money to do this project, when actually it was a shell game every month to see what we could pay for and complete. This wasn’t your usual renovation; it took care and planning and research to get it just right. Every step felt like pushing a ‘55 Buick uphill. But it was worth every cent,” Smith said. Jones died in January 2019, a few months shy of the main renovation being complete, and never lived in the house. It was renamed the Randolph-Lucas-Jones House in his honour.
Article Summary: The Randolph-Lucas-Jones House in Atlanta was built in 1924 for Hollins Nicholas Randolph, the great-great-grandson of Thomas Jefferson. The house was designed by architect P. Thornton Mayre, who also helped build the Fox Theatre. The Randolphs lived there for about a decade before selling it to Margaret Lucas in 1935.

Article Title: A UK collector paid £15 for a broken, lidless teapot at a 2016 auction; experts identified it as one of only seven known John Bartlam pieces, and it sold for £575,000 to The Met in New York
Article Text:
The teapot was about 9cm high and 17.5cm across. Its cover was missing, while the handle had broken off and been restuck.

How the teapot was identified

Another example of John Bartlam's pottery

John Bartlam and his South Carolina pottery

Why the teapot is significant

A UK collector who paid just £15 for a broken, lidless teapot at an auction in 2016 later discovered that the piece was one of the rarest known examples of early American porcelain. The teapot was eventually sold for £575,000, after experts identified it as a piece made by Staffordshire potter John Bartlam in South Carolina in the 1760s.The collector, a private buyer from south-west England, had bought the teapot at a general auction in the Midlands, The Independent reported. It had a broken handle and was missing its lid. At the time, the piece was thought to be Isleworth pottery, made at a factory in Middlesex between 1766 and 1800. However, the buyer was not convinced by that identification.He then took the teapot to Clare Dunham, an expert at Woolley and Wallis auctioneers in Salisbury. Its blue and white decoration, including a distinctive palm tree design, led Dunham to identify it as the work of John Bartlam. Bartlam had left England around 1763 and established a pottery business in South Carolina.The identification changed the significance of the damaged teapot. Experts said it was only the seventh recorded piece of Bartlam porcelain to have reached the market and the only known Bartlam teapot.This made it the earliest American-manufactured teapot to have been discovered.The teapot was then put up for auction by Woolley and Wallis. It was given an estimate of £10,000 to £20,000, while The Independent reported that it was expected to reach as much as £50,000. Instead, bidding pushed the price much higher, with the hammer falling at £460,000.After the buyer’s premium and fees were added, the teapot sold for £575,000. It was bought by London dealer Rod Jellicoe, who was bidding on behalf of The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.The teapot had several features that helped connect it to Bartlam’s pottery. Woolley and Wallis described it as a previously unrecorded American porcelain teapot attributed to John Bartlam and dated it to around 1765–69.The auction house said it was made of porcelain with underglaze blue decoration. One side showed two cranes beneath a tall palm tree, with figures in a sampan and another figure in a separate boat. The other side featured a version of the Man on the Bridge pattern, showing a bridge connecting small islands in a Chinese pagoda landscape.The teapot was about 9cm high and 17.5cm across. Its cover was missing, while the handle had broken off and been restuck.Woolley and Wallis said the teapot had only recently been identified as an example of early American porcelain. It was believed to have been part of a matched tea service that reached England in the late 1760s or 1770s.The auction house also linked the teapot to other pieces associated with Bartlam’s pottery. Four teabowls from the same group had been found to match pieces of pottery excavated at Bartlam’s factory site in Cain Hoy, South Carolina.The teapot was one of only seven recorded pieces of Bartlam porcelain at the time. The other known pieces included four teabowls and two saucers from the same set.Bartlam was trained in Staffordshire, England, and moved to South Carolina around 1763. He established his pottery at Cain Hoy, outside Charleston, with the aim of producing porcelain in America rather than relying on luxury porcelain imported from England.The Met says the teapot was made at Bartlam’s pottery in Cain Hoy around 1765–69. It describes the object as soft-paste porcelain with underglaze blue decoration.The pottery was established at a time when deposits of the special clay needed to make porcelain had recently been discovered in the Carolinas. The clay was being mined and shipped from Charleston to England.Bartlam wanted his business to compete with the luxury porcelain being produced in England and sent to the American colonies. His work therefore represented an attempt to produce similar goods in the colonies.The Met’s records also note that Josiah Wedgwood was concerned about the competition. In a 1767 letter to Thomas Bentley, Wedgwood referred to a “Pottwork in Charles Town” that was using Cherokee clay from the Carolinas to make porcelain.Research and archaeological excavations in the early 1990s later provided evidence of a porcelain factory at Cain Hoy dating to the late 1760s. According to The Met, the factory predates the American China Manufactory established by Gousse Bonnin and George Anthony Morris in Philadelphia in 1770.The teapot is now part of The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s collection and is on view at The Met Fifth Avenue in Gallery 723. The museum identifies John Bartlam as its manufacturer and dates it to around 1765–69.The Met says the object is one of only seven examples that can be associated with Bartlam’s factory. All seven are teawares and feature the palmetto, a motif not found in English porcelains. The palmetto is the state tree of South Carolina and provides a direct connection to the teapot’s American origin.The museum also notes that the teapot has a very white porcelain body and is thinly potted. Its decoration includes landscape scenes in the chinoiserie style, a style that reflected the popularity of Asian-inspired designs in European porcelain at the time.For the collector who originally bought the damaged piece, the discovery was unexpected. He said he had spent decades studying ceramics but had never expected to find such a rare object. “I have been studying ceramics for 30 years and I never dreamt that I would find such a rarity as this teapot,” he said as qouted by The Independent.He also said he was pleased not only with the auction result but with where the teapot would eventually go. “Not only am I extremely pleased for the result for myself, but also because the teapot is going home to America where it will be on public display for generations to come.“I spent a lot of time in the ceramic galleries at the Victoria and Albert Museum when I was first learning about ceramics and just never thought that one day I would have a hand in providing a major museum with such a unique and wonderful object”.Woolley and Wallis said the teapot had “caught the imagination of many” and that it was “absolutely delighted” with the sale.
Article Summary: The teapot was about 9cm high and 17.5cm across. Its cover was missing, while the handle had broken off and been restuck. At the time, the piece was thought to be Isleworth pottery, made at a factory in Middlesex between 1766 and 1800. It was eventually sold for £575,000, after experts identified it as a piece made by Staffordshire potter John Bartlam in South Carolina in 1760s.

Article Title: In 2014, Shonda Rhimes bought a 1923 Hancock Park mansion for $8.8 million; after restoring and expanding it, she sold the 12,000-sq-ft estate for a record $21 million in 2022
Article Text:
Rhimes purchased the mansion from actress Patricia Heaton, best known for Everybody Loves Raymond. Over the following seven years, she undertook an extensive restoration and redesign, turning the historic property into a home that balanced its original character with a more contemporary sense of space and light.

A landmark home gets a new lease of life

Restoring the Italianate villa

A compound built for entertaining

A record-setting sale

There are houses that make a statement, and then there are houses that quietly become part of Los Angeles history. In Hancock Park, one such residence has now added another chapter to its century-old story. Once owned by television producer Shonda Rhimes , the sprawling estate changed hands for $21 million, setting a new record for the Wilshire neighbourhood and marking a remarkable rise from the $8.8 million Rhimes paid for it in 2014, states the Los Angeles Times report.The LA Times report mentions that the estate began its life in 1923, designed by celebrated architect Elmer Grey, whose portfolio also includes the Beverly Hills Hotel and the Huntington Art Gallery. Set across more than an acre and combining two parcels on a prominent corner lot, the property had the scale and architectural pedigree of a grand Los Angeles residence.Rhimes purchased the mansion from actress Patricia Heaton, best known for Everybody Loves Raymond. Over the following seven years, she undertook an extensive restoration and redesign, turning the historic property into a home that balanced its original character with a more contemporary sense of space and light, 2022 online report states.The report also states that working with interior designer Michael Smith, Rhimes moved away from the home's later Santa Barbara mission-style appearance and brought back the Italianate villa aesthetic envisioned by Grey. The renovation was as much about revealing the architecture as it was about updating the interiors. A wood front door was replaced with glass, allowing more natural light into the entryway. The ceiling of the first-floor loggia was removed to create a dramatic two-storey gallery, while glass-blown skylights further opened up the interiors.Inside, marble floors, Venetian plaster, elaborate crown moulding and carefully restored architectural details give the nearly 12,000-square-foot residence a sense of old-world grandeur without making it feel frozen in time.Spread across three floors, the mansion contains seven bedrooms and 10 bathrooms, alongside a formal dining room, two kitchens, a library, playroom and a movie theatre complete with a snack bar. A separate guesthouse adds another unusual feature: a private hair salon, adds the report.The grounds are equally expansive. Two yards, a swimming pool, cabana, paddle tennis court and a secluded hedged garden transform the property into something closer to a private compound than a traditional city home.If we go by the online report, the property was initially listed for $25 million before the asking price was reduced to $23 million. It eventually sold for $21 million, making it the most expensive residential transaction ever recorded in Hancock Park's Wilshire neighborhood. The record had previously been held by Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos, who paid $15.95 million in 2015 for the former home of Antonio Banderas and Melanie Griffith. Sarandos would later play a significant role in Rhimes' career, bringing her to Netflix in 2017 through a major development deal.For Rhimes, the sale adds another notable chapter to an already extensive Los Angeles real estate portfolio. The Shondaland founder, whose television empire includes Grey's Anatomy, Scandal, Bridgerton and How to Get Away With Murder, has owned several properties in Hancock Park and also maintains a Manhattan penthouse. The $21 million sale ultimately reflects more than a celebrity premium. It is a testament to what can happen when historic architecture, thoughtful restoration and a coveted Los Angeles address come together under one roof.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and Facebook
Article Summary: Rhimes purchased the mansion from actress Patricia Heaton, best known for Everybody Loves Raymond. Over the following seven years, she undertook an extensive restoration and redesign, turning the historic property into a home that balanced its original character with a more contemporary sense of space and light.Spread across three floors, the mansion contains seven bedrooms and 10 bathrooms.

Article Title: 526 kg drugs worth Rs 3,000 crore seized from Iranian boat with Pakistani crew
Article Text:
Coast guard intercepts Iranian dhow, seizes 526 kg narcotics worth over Rs 3,000cr
