NEW DELHI: The Indian Coast Guard , in coordination with the Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS), seized approximately 526 kg of narcotics from an Iranian dhow in the Arabian Sea west of Lakshadweep, officials said.The Coast Guard said five Pakistani nationals operating the vessel were also detained during the operation carried out near Lakshadweep on September 25, as reported by news agency PTI.The drugs, valued at over Rs 3,000 crore in the international market, were seized after the vessel was intercepted during the operation.The Coast Guard conducted coordinated sea-air surveillance to track the suspicious vessel before launching a hot pursuit and boarding the dhow.The operation was carried out in coordination with the Gujarat Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) to intercept the vessel. The seized contraband comprised heroin and methamphetamine, while five Pakistani nationals operating the dhow were also apprehended.The dhow, its crew and the seized drugs were escorted to Mumbai under armed security for joint interrogation and further legal proceedings.The operation was part of coordinated efforts by the Coast Guard and Gujarat ATS to detect and disrupt suspected transnational maritime drug-smuggling networks.The seizure comes as Indian maritime and law enforcement agencies continue efforts to prevent narcotics from being smuggled through sea routes. The Coast Guard has previously conducted joint operations with Gujarat ATS and other agencies to intercept vessels suspected of carrying illegal drugs.In April 2025, the Coast Guard, along with Gujarat ATS, seized 307.5 kg of narcotics off the Gujarat coast, according to the Coast Guard's official record of interdiction cases.Several drug-interdiction operations have been conducted along maritime routes in the Arabian Sea, with agencies relying on intelligence inputs, vessel surveillance and coordination between maritime and land-based enforcement units to identify suspected consignments.The Coast Guard said the latest operation underlined its efforts to strengthen maritime surveillance and prevent illicit activities in India's maritime zones. The seized drugs and apprehended crew were brought to Mumbai for further investigation and legal action.
Article Summary: Indian Coast Guard intercepts Iranian dhow, seizes 526 kg narcotics worth over Rs 3,000cr. The seized contraband comprised heroin and methamphetamine. Five Pakistani nationals operating the dhow were also apprehended. The seizure comes as Indian maritime and law enforcement agencies continue efforts to prevent narcotics from being smuggled.

Article Title: Russia backs India's claim to UNSC seat, firmly shuts door on Germany & Japan
Article Text:
Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly (Photo: Reuters).

Russia on Saturday backed a permanent seat for India and Brazil on the United Nations Security Council, while strongly opposing the same for Western countries.During his speech at the General Assembly, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said no additional seats at the UNSC should be given to Western countries, especially to Germany and the US ally, Japan.Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India’s bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council . Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.Lavrov has previously argued that the current composition no longer reflects today’s global balance and explicitly endorsed India, alongside Brazil, for permanent membership.This support was reiterated in the 2026 BRICS New Delhi Declaration, with China and Russia backing India and Brazil for a greater role in the UN, including the Security Council.Lavrov accused the West of continuously pumping weapons into Ukraine while helping target drones and missiles at Russia's civilians and civilian infrastructure.He also mentioned that Europe raised an anti-Moscow regime in Kyivv, in order to control the Russian influence."To pursue a utopian goal of containing Russia, the West dismantled the European security system and cultivated a Russophobic regime in Kyiv," he said, while warning the Western nations of "consequences".He further accused Europe of doing everything to block a peaceful settlement with Ukraine and disrupt negotiation prospects favoured by many, including the Trump administration.Lavrov claimed several EU leaders of being infected with racial superiority, encouraging the rise of what he called Ukrainian Nazism.The Russian foreign minister said the UN’s core principles were being put at risk, with the West overlooking the spread of Nazism in Ukraine.
Article Summary: Russia has been one of the most consistent supporters of India's bid for a permanent seat on the UN Security Council. Moscow has repeatedly backed India’s candidature as part of a broader push to make the Council more representative of Asia, Africa and Latin America.

Article Title: Green Card holder's mother denied B1/B2 visa to attend housewarming ceremony: They did not ask for any documents
Article Text:
A Green Card holder says her mother was denied B1/B2 visa in Mumbai.

What went wrong?

An Indian woman with US Green Card shared the experience of a B1/B2 visa interview at Mumbai Consulate attended by her mother which ended in a flat refusal. As the woman shared her mother's interview experience, seeking advice on what they did wrong, it emerged as an interesting case to study for B1/B2 visa applicants, as the denial rates in India are quite high. Whenever visa officers don't find strong ties of the applicants with India, they deny visa detecting "immigration intent" which means that they suspect that the applicants may not return to India.In this case, as specified by the Reddit post, the visa officer asked the mother, a widow staying in India with her son while the daughter is a US Green Card holder with a US citizen spouse, the purpose of her visit. The mother had no history of international travel and it was her first intended trip to the US to attend the housewarming ceremony of the daughter.The trip was planned for a month. The visa officer asked her about the funding of the trip. The mother, a widowed housewife, said she was funding the trip herself through savings. "I have my savings good enough to cover my one month trip. I live with my son so he takes care of my expenses and I also survive out of the interest from my FD and other investments. I also do some small embroidery work but it's seasonal and not often available," the mother said."They didn't ask for any documents. my mother has property and all the investments on her name. I don't know what went wrong here," the Redditor said. Within five minutes of this conversation, the visa was denied. The visa officer also told her to apply again.Redditors pointed out that though a similar case may get approved in another consulate or by a different visa officer, the mother did not actually show any strong ties to India. A widow with no job and a richer child in the US is a person who has fewer chances to go back to India
Article Summary: A Green Card holder says her mother was denied B1/B2 visa in Mumbai. The mother, a widowed housewife, said she was funding the trip herself through savings. Within five minutes of this conversation, the visa was denied. The visa officer also told her to apply again.

Article Title: In 2024, 75-year-old Iowa farmer Evie Haupt said three wind turbines on her 160 acres were bringing in about $35,000 a year while using under 3 acres and had helped reduce $350,000 in farm debt to $67
Article Text:
A financial lifeline for rural landowners

The explosive expansion of Iowa wind power

Addressing local pushback and debate

On a 160-acre farm in central Iowa, three tall wind turbines quietly rise above the fields. Each turbine uses less than an acre of land, but together they provide an annual income that has changed the financial future of 75-year-old farmer Evie Haupt. According to a CBS News report by Janet Shamlian and Alicia Hastey, Haupt earns about $35,000 each year by leasing part of her land for the wind turbines. The income rises with inflation and has helped her pay down a $350,000 farm debt left after her husband died a decade ago. Her remaining debt is now $67,000. For many family farms across the United States, extra sources of income have become important lifelines. The U.S. Department of Agriculture expects farm profits to fall by 25 per cent, as farmers face higher costs, changing crop prices and unpredictable weather. Adding wind power to traditional farming can provide steady income and help protect farmers from financial shocks.Farm debt can leave families with difficult choices, including selling land that has been in the family for generations. Haupt faced this situation after her husband died and left her with hundreds of thousands of dollars in farm debt.Payments from the wind turbines provided her with a regular source of income that she could use to repay the loans. Each turbine takes up less than an acre, allowing Haupt to continue farming most of her 160 acres. This means the same land provides her with two sources of income while only a small portion is used for the turbines. The payments can also increase over time because the contracts include inflation adjustments, helping landowners manage rising prices and other costs. For Haupt, the arrangement has made a significant difference. She has now paid off more than 80% of her farm debt while continuing to use the land for farming.Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Iowa had only a few hundred wind turbines 20 years ago. Today, it has more than 6,000, producing about 60 per cent of the state's energy. Across the United States, more than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Federal energy officials also say current U.S. wind power cuts carbon emissions by an amount equal to taking 73 million passenger vehicles off the road. Attorney Kathy Law, who grew up on a farm and married a farmer, has helped place nearly half of Iowa's wind turbines. Her work in energy law grew from her own family's experience with farming. Law wanted to study law while she was in high school, but the severe farm crisis of the 1980s kept her home to help with the family farm. She later went to law school in her forties. She graduated on the same day her son finished high school and later served as president of the Iowa Wind Energy Association for three years. "From my farm background, I think I can talk their talk and have conversations with landowners that are interested in having wind turbines on their property," Law told CBS News.The rapid growth of wind power in rural communities has also brought opposition in some counties. Local critics say wind turbines can change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats. Law believes landowners should be able to decide what happens on their property. "Nobody's requiring them to put that on their farms or on their land," Law said during her interview with CBS News. "We want to be able to put turbines on our land and receive those benefits. " Haupt has a similar view of the changes to her farm. While she remains attached to traditional farming, she sees clean energy as an important step for rural communities. "I look at it as progress," Haupt told CBS News. "I think we can't stand in the way of progress." For Haupt, giving up a very small part of her land to produce electricity makes sense for her finances and for the wider community. "I need to give up one or two acres of my land so that I can generate a commodity that we all use every day, and we all want to use more of it every day," Haupt said. "So I'm happy to be able to be a part of that generation."
Article Summary: Iowa has become a major wind energy state over the past two decades. More than 70,000 land-based wind turbines are operating in the U.S. Nationwide, wind power supplies about 10 per cent of the electric grid. Critics say wind turbines change scenic views, create unwanted noise and threaten birds and bats.

Article Title: ‘Wake up’: Iran releases 25-page letter urging US voters to reject Trump ahead of midterms
Article Text:
The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections

‘Wake up’: Iran takes message to US voters

‘Death to America’ explained as attack on rulers

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that Iran's appeal to American voters will influence the outcome of the midterm elections? Yes, it will have a significant impact No, it will not influence the elections Possibly, but only to a limited extent 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to American voters, urging them to reject President Donald Trump ’s policies and “wrest control back from corrupt politicians” as the US heads towards its midterm elections. In a lengthy open letter addressed to the American public, the powerful Iranian military force argued that Washington’s war against Iran had failed to achieve its objectives and called for a change in US policy towards Tehran.The 25-page letter, released seven months after the US-Israel war against Iran began, seeks to draw a distinction between the American people and their government. The IRGC argues that ordinary Iranians and Americans share common interests and grievances, portraying both as victims of political leaders pursuing costly wars. It also urges Americans to oppose US support for Israel and foreign military interventions, while presenting peaceful coexistence between Washington and Tehran as possible if US policy changes.IRGC spokesman Gen Hossein Mohebbi reinforced the message at a news conference in Tehran on Tuesday, saying the only way for the conflict to end was for Washington to acknowledge defeat and withdraw. He urged Americans to reconsider their leadership and put pressure on the Trump administration, arguing that many US citizens remained unaware of what he described as the “harms” caused by its policies.The timing of the letter is significant. The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections, with the IRGC describing the current period as a moment when the American political system is at its weakest. Mohebbi said he did not necessarily expect the letter to change the US administration’s behaviour, but hoped American voters would hear its message.The letter repeatedly attacks Trump’s justification for the war, particularly his claim that Iran’s nuclear programme posed a threat that required military action. Tehran has consistently denied seeking nuclear weapons and maintains that its uranium enrichment programme has civilian purposes.“The enemy [US] knows that Iran is not after nuclear weapons,” Mohebbi said, echoing the letter’s argument that Washington has used the nuclear issue as a pretext to pursue wider strategic and economic goals.The IRGC also claims that the US and Israel failed to achieve their stated objectives in the war. According to the letter, the targets shifted repeatedly after earlier goals, including regime change and partition of Iran, were not achieved. It lists objectives ranging from forcing Iran’s unconditional surrender and destroying its nuclear and missile programmes to taking control of the Strait of Hormuz.The letter declares Iran the victor, claiming that thousands of US and Israeli strikes damaged Iranian infrastructure but failed to accomplish their stated aims. It further claims that Iranian forces inflicted major losses on US military assets and severely damaged American bases across the region. These assertions are presented by the IRGC as evidence of a broader strategic defeat for Washington.The Strait of Hormuz features prominently in the letter and Mohebbi’s remarks. He rejected US claims that Iran had lost its leverage over the vital waterway, arguing that the movement of a limited number of vessels did not mean the strait was fully open. Oil exports through the waterway, however, have recovered substantially from the levels seen earlier in the conflict, according to figures cited in the supplied material.The IRGC letter also attempts to explain one of the most recognisable slogans associated with Iran’s political system: “Death to America”. It argues that the phrase is directed at the US political establishment rather than the American population.“‘Death to America’ is a prayer for the eradication of the diabolical ruling elite whose seat of power is the White House,” the letter says.The document repeatedly contrasts the American public with Washington’s political leadership, claiming that taxpayers ultimately bear the financial burden of US wars. It asks Americans to question why their government continues to pursue military confrontation and warns of what it describes as the consequences of an ongoing conflict.The IRGC’s approach echoes Cold War-era efforts to reach an adversary’s population directly. During the Vietnam War, Vietnamese broadcaster Trinh Thi Ngo, widely known as “Hanoi Hannah”, used English-language broadcasts to target American troops, urging them to question their government and the war. Her programmes highlighted US casualties, anti-war protests and reports critical of the conflict while presenting the Vietnamese side’s narrative.Iran has similarly sought to communicate directly with Western audiences since the latest war began, using Iran-linked media and online networks, including English-language AI-generated videos, memes and short-form content.The IRGC letter now represents a much more formal version of that strategy: an attempt to speak past Washington and directly to American voters.For Tehran, the central message is that the war is not simply a military confrontation between two states, but a political choice that Americans themselves can challenge. Mohebbi urged them to put pressure on their government, while the letter concluded with a broader argument that Iran’s resistance had demonstrated the limits of American military power.Meanwhile, Iran’s economic pressures remain severe. The rial fell to a new record low on Tuesday, with traders in Tehran reportedly exchanging more than 2.5 million rials for one US dollar. The currency has repeatedly hit new lows since the war began.
Article Summary: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to American voters, urging them to reject President Donald Trump ’s policies. The 25-page letter, released seven months after the US-Israel war against Iran began, seeks to draw a distinction between the American people and their government. The IRGC argues that ordinary Iranians and Americans share common interests and grievances.

Article Title: ‘Time for trial and error is over’: OpenAI safety employee David Robinson quits over AI risks
Article Text:
David Robinson made the comments in an article titled "I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken".

A former OpenAI safety employee has resigned from the company, warning that its rapid development of increasingly capable AI systems could raise the risk of serious failures. David Robinson said the “time for trial and error is over” and argued that AI companies need to put far greater emphasis on safety before developing more powerful systems.Robinson made the comments in an article titled "I Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken", published by The Atlantic on Saturday.Robinson said AI companies, including OpenAI, were not being "nearly careful enough" and argued that safety research and expertise should play a much bigger role before more powerful AI systems are developed.Robinson spent 3-1/2 years at OpenAI, where he helped draft the company's preparedness framework and oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier-model launches. He said the company's focus on moving quickly from one AI model launch to another was making it difficult to maintain the level of caution he believed was necessary."As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed."He argued that the development of advanced AI should no longer rely on a process of repeatedly releasing systems, finding problems and fixing them afterwards.OpenAI refers to this approach as "iterative deployment", under which systems are released and their safeguards are strengthened as new problems are identified.Robinson argued that this approach is no longer sufficient as AI systems become more powerful."The time for trial and error is over," he wrote, saying advanced AI systems should have safeguards comparable to those used in high-risk fields such as nuclear power and aviation.His criticism comes amid a wider debate in the AI industry over whether companies are developing increasingly powerful systems faster than their ability to understand and control them. OpenAI and rival Anthropic have both faced scrutiny following incidents involving failed safety controls or unexpected behaviour from experimental AI systems.Robinson also warned that AI capabilities are advancing faster than researchers' understanding of alignment. AI alignment refers to efforts to ensure that AI systems behave in ways that are consistent with human goals and values.OpenAI defended its approach, saying it continues to put safety measures in place and can slow development when necessary."We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down," an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement.
Article Summary: David Robinson said the “time for trial and error is over” and argued that AI companies need to put far greater emphasis on safety. Robinson spent 3-1/2 years at OpenAI, where he helped draft the company's preparedness framework and oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier-model launches.

Article Title: California sanctuary is removing purple sea urchins to help restore kelp; 117,847 pounds have been added to compost
Article Text:
PC: Steve Lonhart/NOAA

How are purple urchins being removed and turned into compost

PC: Matt Lauchenauer/Dandy Fish Company/ National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)

Why are purple urchins being removed from kelp restoration sites

Why are starving purple urchins composted instead of sold as seafood

Purple urchins turn marine nutrients into compost for farms

California sanctuary is removing purple sea urchins from areas targeted for kelp restoration and giving them a second use as compost. Since 2023, urchins collected from restoration sites in Greater Farallones National Marine Sanctuary have been transported to West Marin Compost in Marin County.Removing the urchins helps reduce their numbers near bull kelp, which gives the kelp a better chance to survive, reach adulthood, and release spores. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), a total of 117,847 pounds of purple urchins have been added to the compost mix as of July 2025. The animals also provide nitrogen, calcium, and micronutrients that enrich compost used by local farmers and gardeners.The purple urchins are harvested by hand from areas selected for their high potential for kelp restoration. The effort is led by the Greater Farallones Association, along with Greater Farallones and Cordell Bank National Marine Sanctuaries. After being collected, the urchins are transported to West Marin Compost, where they are added to the compost mix. Since 2023, 117,847 pounds of urchins have been added to the compost.Reducing the number of purple urchins around bull kelp gives the plants more opportunity to survive, mature, and release spores that can produce the next generation. Commercial urchin diver Erik Owen has been collecting the animals for the restoration project since 2023. The harvested urchins are then taken to West Marin Compost, where they become part of the composting process.Purple urchins feed on kelp, and their numbers can rise sharply when kelp forests decline because of different stressors. Greater Farallones National Marine Sanctuary has experienced a catastrophic loss of bull kelp since 2014 following a series of events. As the kelp declined, purple urchins became a dominant part of the nearshore environment and continued feeding on the remaining bull kelp. The restoration effort focuses on areas where kelp has a strong chance of recovery.Purple urchins collected during the restoration work have little commercial value because they are starving after losing much of their bull kelp food supply. They may remain in this condition for years and produce very little uni, a prized delicacy once obtained from healthy red urchins in the sanctuary and along the Sonoma and Mendocino coasts before the major kelp die-off.Local divers collect the urchins at restoration sites and send them for composting instead of exporting these animals for food. This gives the animals another purpose while supporting the restoration effort. Once composted, the urchins become part of material used to grow food, connecting kelp restoration with local agriculture.At West Marin Compost, the harvested urchins add nutrients to compost used by local agriculture. Jeff Creque, a consultant with West Marin Compost, said,"Urchins are a great source of nitrogen, calcium, and micronutrients. We are happy to have a bit of the sea added to our material". The composting effort gives the purple urchins collected from kelp restoration areas a new purpose by turning them into material that can support farmers and gardeners.The wider restoration project also involves work with Northern California’s Tribal community, research at sites where kelp has persisted, collaboration with commercial urchin divers to remove urchins from restoration areas, and kelp outplanting. Together, these activities support the broader effort to restore the ecosystem.
Article Summary: California sanctuary is removing purple sea urchins from areas targeted for kelp restoration and giving them a second use as compost. The animals provide nitrogen, calcium, and micronutrients that enrich compost used by local farmers and gardeners. Since 2023, 117,847 pounds of urchin have been added to the compost mix.

Article Title: Portland is covering ordinary traffic signal boxes with colourful artwork, but it is not just for decoration
Article Text:
Portland is giving ordinary traffic signal boxes a colourful new purpose, covering the metal cabinets with artwork. Image Credit: Meira Gebel/Axios

Why Portland is covering traffic signal boxes with colourful artwork

The project centres on traffic signal boxes and utility cabinets that contain electrical equipment used to operate traffic lights, pedestrian crossings and other traffic functions. Image Credit: Meira Gebel/Axios

The artwork also has a practical purpose

Portland has tested the idea through community art

Student artists helped turn one box into a local landmark

One Portland neighbourhood has linked the art with its surroundings

Lloyd EcoDistrict worked with local artist Irene Ramirez and the city to wrap a utility box near one of Portland’s busiest cycling areas. The artwork focuses on local pollinators and includes the name of Peace Memorial Park. Image Credit: Lloyd EcoDistrict/Website

Portland is making small infrastructure part of the streetscape

Portland is giving ordinary traffic signal boxes a colourful new purpose, covering the metal cabinets with artwork that does more than brighten street corners. The city is using durable vinyl wraps to make these pieces of essential infrastructure more attractive while testing whether the coverings can also discourage graffiti and reduce the need for repeated repainting. The approach has already produced dozens of designs across Portland, from roses and clouds to animals and comic-style images, turning objects that once faded in the background into small pieces of public art.The project centres on traffic signal boxes and utility cabinets that contain electrical equipment used to operate traffic lights, pedestrian crossings and other traffic functions. They are often positioned at busy intersections, along narrow pavements and beside places where people wait for public transport or spend time on foot.According to Axios, Portland’s Public Environment Management Office began wrapping utility boxes with graffiti-resistant vinyl coverings in 2025. The office was created during the pandemic to address visible quality-of-life issues such as graffiti, rubbish and neglected public spaces. The signal-wrap project was developed as one way of dealing with both the appearance and maintenance of these highly visible boxes.The change is noticeable because many of the boxes had previously been repeatedly tagged and then painted over. Those repairs could leave mismatched patches of paint across the metal surfaces. The new coverings provide a consistent design instead of another layer of plain paint.The colourful designs are not simply being added to make intersections look better. The vinyl is intended to resist graffiti, giving the city an opportunity to see whether a more durable surface can reduce the amount of cleaning and repainting required over time.Axios reported that Portland had 130 wrapped signal boxes, with nearly 50 more in development, and more than a dozen designs in use. The average installation cost was about $1,750. The city is continuing to monitor the wraps to determine whether they can provide a financial benefit by reducing long-term maintenance work.The designs themselves vary widely. Some feature oversized roses, clouds and comic-book-style graphics, while others include animals, cartoon characters and lumberjack imagery. There are also Portland Trail Blazers-themed designs, giving some of the otherwise ordinary street equipment a connection to the city’s sporting culture.The current effort builds on an idea that has appeared in Portland communities before. In 2016, the Portland Bureau of Transportation supported a pilot project in East Portland that used a traffic signal box as a small public artwork.A Portland Bureau of Transportation news advisory from November 2016 said residents and local stakeholders had expressed a strong desire for public art during discussions about the future of the Division Midway business district. The Division Midway Alliance researched low-cost approaches and developed the ‘Art on the Box’ concept, which was intended both to beautify the area and deter graffiti.The first installation was placed at Southeast 122nd Avenue and Division Street. The Portland Bureau of Transportation described it as the city’s first use of a traffic signal box for low-cost public art. Its four panels represented the seasons and local culture, including the cultural diversity of the Division Midway area.East Portland News reported that the earlier project involved students from David Douglas High School’s main and Fir Ridge campuses, working under the direction of an adult art coordinator. Their designs were created at school and transferred digitally to a durable vinyl wrap.The resulting artwork replaced a formerly grey electrical utility box with a collection of student-created images. The material, commonly used on vehicles such as trucks and buses, provided a practical surface for the artwork while allowing the box to continue serving its original purpose. The project also showed how a relatively small object could provide an accessible place for young artists to contribute to their neighbourhood.A more recent example can be found at Peace Memorial Park in Portland’s Lloyd neighbourhood. According to Lloyd EcoDistrict, the organisation worked with local artist Irene Ramirez and the city to wrap a utility box near one of Portland’s busiest cycling areas.The artwork focuses on local pollinators and includes the name of Peace Memorial Park. The box had previously been blank and covered in graffiti. The new design was intended to give the location a stronger sense of place while offering cyclists, pedestrians and visitors something colourful to notice as they passed.The Lloyd EcoDistrict also tested the wrap shortly after installation. During a community clean-up, a small amount of graffiti that had appeared on the artwork was removed with an eco-friendly cleaner. The organisation said the graffiti-resistant vinyl could be maintained with a simple wipe-down rather than requiring the whole surface to be repainted.The idea has also been used in Portland, Maine, showing that utility boxes can serve as small public canvases in more than one city with the same name. A 2016 report from News Center Maine described a project in which local artists painted utility boxes around downtown Portland to make otherwise plain infrastructure more attractive. The city said the effort was intended to beautify the urban landscape, encourage civic participation and support local artists.
Article Summary: The project centres on traffic signal boxes and utility cabinets that contain electrical equipment used to operate traffic lights, pedestrian crossings and other traffic functions. The city is using durable vinyl wraps to make these pieces of essential infrastructure more attractive while testing whether the coverings can also discourage graffiti. The approach has already produced dozens of designs across Portland, from roses and clouds to animals and comic-style images.

Article Title: A family foundation began restoring 250 acres of overworked Ohio farmland in 1989; it is now a wildlife reserve with Walden Pond
Article Text:
The Diehl family’s 1989 project reshaped 250 acres of Ohio farmland

A man-made pond became part of the landscape

The 250-acre reserve opens its restored habitats to visitors

PC: Thoreau Wildlife Reserve

Bird nesting becomes part of the reserve’s restoration work

The reserve opened to visitors in 2020

A decades-long transformation created today’s wildlife reserve

At first glance, Thoreau Wildlife Reserve looks less like a former farm and more like a patchwork of Ohio landscapes. Meadows give way to woodland, wetlands sit alongside prairie, and older sections of forest provide another layer of habitat. Across roughly 250 acres, two miles of walking trails now lead visitors through these different settings. Yet the land did not begin this way. In 1989, the Diehl Family Foundation began a long restoration effort on farmland that had been heavily worked. More than 30 years later, the property includes a pond created by a dam, planted woodland and areas allowed to develop into more natural habitats. The reserve opened to the public in 2020.The transformation began in 1989, when the Diehl Family Foundation started a programme intended to change the character of the 250-acre property. The farmland had been heavily used, so the first stage involved preparing the soil for a different kind of landscape.According to Thoreau Wildlife Reserve, that autumn, work began on the ground itself. The following year, a dam was constructed to hold water and create what is now known as Walden Pond.A meadow was seeded, prairie was established and the first trees for a pine plantation went into the soil.The changes were not completed in a single planting season. The project continued for years as the landowners, family members, local workers and volunteers carried out further work across the property.Walden Pond is one of the clearest examples of how the reserve's present landscape was deliberately created. The water body was formed after the dam was built as part of the early restoration work. Around it, the character of the property gradually became more varied. Wetlands, prairie, hardwood woodland and areas of old growth forest now occupy parts of the reserve. Rather than replacing the farmland with one uniform type of planting, the long-running project resulted in several distinct habitats across the site.The changes also created space for a range of plants and wildlife. The reserve sits among a landscape still dominated in part by farmland, making the restored property a contrasting area of habitat.Visitors can now explore the reserve on four nature trails covering about two miles. The routes pass through meadows, woodlands, wetlands and old growth forest, giving the property several different settings within the same 250-acre site. The reserve has also been used for educational purposes. Students and faculty from Defiance College have carried out ecology studies on the property over the years, adding an academic use to the land alongside its role as a wildlife habitat.Signs placed along the trails also feature thoughts associated with H.D. Thoreau, whose ideas and writing inspired the name of the reserve.The restoration effort has extended beyond trees and vegetation. Thoreau Wildlife Reserve works with the Audubon Sanctuary Program to encourage several bird species to nest on the property, including bluebirds, wood ducks and mallard ducks.The different habitats provide a mixture of conditions across the reserve. Wet areas, woodland and open spaces each form part of the wider landscape, while the continued management of the property is intended to support wildlife living and nesting there.Although the land had been undergoing changes for decades, public access came much later. In 2020, after years of preparation, Thoreau Wildlife Reserve opened its trails to visitors. The stated purpose was to make the property available for education, recreation and appreciation of the natural environment while maintaining its role as a refuge for plants and wildlife. Opening the land also marked a new stage in a project that had begun with soil preparation and planting more than 30 years earlier.Today, access remains fairly controlled. The reserve is open from dawn until dusk, with parking available but limited. Visitors are required to remain on the designated trails, and only walking is permitted within the preserve. Dogs can be brought in, but they must remain on a lead.Visitors are asked to follow leave-no-trace principles and respect the site's natural resources. The restrictions are part of how the reserve manages public access while keeping the restored habitats intact. The property is located at 10485 Haller Road and covers approximately 250 acres. What began in 1989 as an effort to change the condition and use of heavily worked farmland has since developed into a mixture of planted and naturally developing habitats, centred partly around the man-made Walden Pond.The landscape is therefore the product of a long process rather than a single restoration project. Fields were prepared, water was held behind a new dam, trees and prairie were planted, and subsequent decades of work gradually changed the character of the property. By the time the public arrived in 2020, the site had become a wildlife reserve with trails running through several distinct ecosystems.
Article Summary: Thoreau Wildlife Reserve opened to the public in 2020 after a decades-long restoration effort. The property includes a pond created by a dam, planted woodland and areas allowed to develop into more natural habitats. Meadows give way to woodland, wetlands sit alongside prairie and older sections of forest provide another layer of habitat.

Article Title: Beavers beat humans to restoring a closed Massachusetts golf course, building a 6-to-8-foot dam before crews arrived
Article Text:
Image: James Paleologopoulos/WAMC

How the Pine Grove golf course drained the land

Old Wilson Way between Rocky Hill and Florence roads (Image: James Paleologopoulos/WAMC)

The beaver dam that arrived before the machines

What human crews are doing along the brook

Funding, trails, and a model for other courses

When a Massachusetts golf course closes, the land does not stay quiet for long. At the former Pine Grove Golf Course in Northampton, beavers moved in roughly a year before restoration crews, damming a small stream with a wall of mud and sticks six to eight feet tall. According to WAMC Northeast Public Radio, the new pond is already drawing wood ducks and swallows back to the site. Meanwhile, the city and state ecologists are ripping up pavement and reshaping the brook, in what project partners call a flagship example of golf course rewilding, a model for other retired courses.Golf courses have been closing across the Northeast, and especially in Massachusetts. WAMC cites a Boston Business Journal estimate that at least 57 courses closed in the state between 2012 and 2022. Northampton acquired Pine Grove in 2020. The course once had 18 holes, a clubhouse, and a small pond, and Sarah LaValley of the city's Office of Planning and Sustainability told the station the owner had hoped for years that another golf group would take over before the city stepped in.Tom Lautzenheiser, a senior conservation ecologist with the Massachusetts Audubon Society, explained to WAMC why the green fairways were not good for the environment.Because golfers want dry ground, water was channelled through cisterns and trench drains and sent straight to Nashawannuck Brook, then downstream toward the Arcadia wildlife sanctuary. In a watershed of roughly 300 acres, about 100 acres were golf course, and Lautzenheiser said the grass behaved like pavement.Kate Bentsen, an ecological restoration specialist with the state Division of Ecological Restoration, told WAMC that human work was only getting underway while the local beavers had started their own restoration at least a year earlier. She described a very small stream that has been flooded by a large dam, which began developing about a year ago and stands somewhere between six and eight feet tall, impounding a considerable area.The results are visible. Bentsen said birds are returning, including wood ducks and swallows. According to the WAMC report, the wall of mud and sticks is close to impenetrable, yet a healthy stream still flows through its base, keeping water in the habitat during mild drought conditions.The human work is large too. WAMC reports that heavy machinery has spent at least a month tearing up the road along Old Wilson Way between Rocky Hill and Florence roads, which LaValley described as the city's first ecologically related road closure. Travis Sumner of SumCo Eco-Contracting said phase one has already removed over 800 feet of pavement and will restore 1,600 feet of the stream by taking out the rock-lined channel that rushes water off the site, with much of the work hoped to be finished by the end of June. The public was asked to stay out until July 1.Phase two, according to LaValley, includes removing a man-made dam at a nearby irrigation pond, which is not the beaver dam, plus more wetland and trail work. Planners also hope to build an accessible loop called the All Persons Trail, with a bridge over a culvert that has failed. Tom Annese, a land planning assistant for Northampton, told WAMC that the open character of the site is rare among the city's mostly wooded, hilly conservation land, and that its wet conditions made housing mostly impractical.Recent work was funded in part by the state division and the city, totalling at least $720,000. Later construction could cost as much as $3 million, and LaValley said she is optimistic about winning more state grants while acknowledging that plans may need rethinking if the money does not come through.Project partners see wider significance. Julianne Busa of the engineering and design firm Fuss & O'Neill told WAMC that Pine Grove is the first project of its kind in Massachusetts and that the state division hopes it will serve as a flagship for rewilding retired courses. Similar efforts are following, she said, including a driving range being rewilded in Stow and the Beaver Brook project in Williamsburg and Northampton.That second project belongs to The Trustees, the Massachusetts conservation organisation, which acquired the Beaver Brook Golf Course in July 2025. The Trustees also says it is learning from regional golf course restoration projects, naming Pine Grove and its Nashawannuck Brook work among them.David Eisenhauer of the state division told WAMC that the work is not so much creating something new as returning something that was always there, a connection between people and nature.
Article Summary: Pine Grove Golf Course in Northampton, Massachusetts, closed in 2012. Beavers moved in roughly a year before restoration crews, damming a small stream with a wall of mud and sticks six to eight feet tall. The city and state ecologists are ripping up pavement and reshaping the brook, in what project partners call a flagship example of golf course rewilding.

Article Title: Trump leaks senator’s number after row over clock-change bill: What’s the dispute
Article Text:
Trump posted what he said was Cotton’s cellphone number on social media.

What is Trump proposing

Why is Cotton opposing it

Trump asks voters to call Cotton

Why does the issue matter

US President Donald Trump has publicly clashed with fellow Republican Senator Tom Cotton over a proposal to keep daylight saving time in place throughout the year.The dispute took an unusual turn on Saturday when Trump posted what he said was Cotton’s cellphone number on social media and asked people in Arkansas to call the senator and pressure him to support the proposal.The move came after Trump accused Cotton of holding up the Sunshine Protection Act, a bill that would stop Americans from changing their clocks twice a year.Under the current system, Americans move their clocks one hour forward in March and one hour back in November.Moving the clock forward means sunrise and sunset appear one hour later on the clock. For example, if the sun would normally rise at 7 am and set at 6 pm, the clock change would make them appear as 8 am and 7 pm. This gives people more daylight in the evening.Trump wants the March setting to remain in place throughout the year. That means Americans would not move their clocks back in November.Trump has repeatedly criticised the twice-yearly clock change, calling it “ridiculous”. On Saturday, he said the practice “discombobulates everybody.”The Sunshine Protection Act passed the House of Representatives in July by 308 votes to 117 but has remained stalled in the Senate.Cotton, who represents Arkansas, says keeping daylight saving time throughout the year would make winter mornings too dark.He pointed to an earlier attempt to adopt permanent daylight saving time in the US. The country tried it in 1974, but public support quickly fell as people complained about late sunrises during winter. The change was abandoned in less than a year.“No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter,” Mr. Cotton said in a social media post. “Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark.”Cotton's position puts him at odds with Trump despite the two Republicans generally being political allies.Trump included a letter from PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp in his post supporting the bill. Rolapp argued that an extra hour of daylight in the evening could allow Americans to play 23 million additional rounds of golf each year.Trump urged people in Arkansas to contact Cotton directly.“To the Great People of Arkansas, please let your Senator know it would be a GREAT Bipartisan WIN for the United States Senate,” Mr. Trump said. “Call Tom on his cellphone.”Two officials confirmed that the number Trump posted belonged to Cotton. His office did not respond to a request for comment. Calls to the number went to an automated message saying the recipient was “temporarily unavailable.”Cotton later defended his position without directly referring to Trump's post. Trump responded within an hour, accusing Cotton of blocking the bill and asking why he was doing so, other than “ego?”The debate is not simply about whether Americans prefer longer evenings. Many sleep scientists favour the existing system because morning sunlight helps keep people's body clocks aligned with the natural day.The 1974 experiment is also central to the argument. Supporters of permanent daylight saving time say the extra evening light would benefit activities such as sports and leisure, while opponents warn that winter mornings could become significantly darker. Trump has previously used a similar tactic against another senator.During the 2016 Republican presidential primary, he publicly displayed the phone number of Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, who was then competing against him for the Republican nomination, and encouraged people to call him.At Graham's funeral in July, Trump acknowledged that sharing the number was something he “shouldn’t have done.”“And I remember the number,” Mr. Trump said, reciting the digits again at the funeral. “If anybody wants to give it a shot,” he added.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has publicly clashed with fellow Republican Senator Tom Cotton over a proposal to keep daylight saving time in place throughout the year. Trump posted what he said was Cotton’s cellphone number on social media and asked people in Arkansas to call the senator. The move came after Trump accused Cotton of holding up the Sunshine Protection Act.

Article Title: US 'kicks out' Iranian diplomats after defying earlier order amid stalled talks: Report
Article Text:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrives ahead of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

Two Iranian diplomats were expelled from the US after allegedly defying a state department order to leave the country following the UN General Assembly, accordng to a report by Axios.The diplomats, who were part of Iran’s delegation to the UN General Assembly in New York, were asked on Monday to leave the US along with the rest of the delegation. However, they remained in New York for several days, the official said.“Secretary Rubio means business. Two more members of the Iranian delegation were found still in New York long after the UN General Assembly had passed. They have now been kicked out of the country,” the US official said.On Friday, the Iranian mission to the UN was informed that US authorities were aware the two diplomats were still in New York and were again ordered to leave immediately.One of the diplomats left the US on Friday night, while the second departed on Saturday morning, according to the official.The move comes amid heightened tensions between Washington and Tehran, with diplomatic efforts to end the war faltering and concerns growing over a possible resumption of fighting.However, the Iranian mission earlier said the delegation’s departure was scheduled in advance and that the plan had been communicated to the US State Department."Araghchi had already been scheduled to leave New York on Monday night," reported AP. While US officials said that Rubio ordered Araghchi and his delegation to leave the city earlier than planned.
Article Summary: Two Iranian diplomats were expelled from the US after allegedly defying a state department order to leave the country. The diplomats were part of Iran’s delegation to the UN General Assembly in New York. The move comes amid heightened tensions between Washington and Tehran.

Article Title: A radioactive material facility polluted an Illinois creek for decades; the 6.7-mile Superfund site has now been removed from the cleanup list
Article Text:
Representative Image of a serene wetland nature reserve with ponds and wildlife, replacing a former golf course (AI Generated Image)

How the Rare Earths Facility contaminated Kress Creek

Crews removed contaminated soil and sediment

Kress Creek was one of four Superfund sites

What National Priorities List deletion means

A 6.7-mile stretch of creek and river in DuPage County, Illinois, has reached a major milestone after decades of radioactive contamination linked to a former industrial facility. The US Environmental Protection Agency deleted the Kerr-McGee Kress Creek/West Branch DuPage River Superfund site from the National Priorities List in August 2026, meaning the site no longer requires further Superfund response action to protect human health and the environment. The contamination was linked to the former Rare Earths Facility in West Chicago, which operated from 1932 to 1973 and processed rare earth elements and radioactive materials, as well as producing gas lantern mantles. Radioactive surface runoff from the facility entered Kress Creek, while thorium-containing material spread through the sediment and banks of the creek and the West Branch of the DuPage River, as well as some surrounding floodplain areas. This remarkable environmental recovery demonstrates how sustained, decades-long remediation efforts can successfully restore contaminated waterways, offering communities renewed confidence in their local ecosystems' long-term health and safety.The former facility was operated by Lindsay Light and Chemical Company and later by other companies, including Kerr-McGee. Its operations involved processing rare earth ores and radioactive materials, including thorium. Waste generated during those activities became part of a much larger environmental cleanup in the West Chicago area.The Kress Creek site was placed on the National Priorities List in 1991. EPA describes the Superfund site as covering approximately 6.7 miles, including Kress Creek and the West Branch of the DuPage River. Radioactively contaminated material was found in creek sediments, along streambanks and in portions of the floodplain. The contamination was part of a wider legacy from the former Rare Earths Facility. Four separate West Chicago-area sites associated with radioactive waste from the facility were ultimately placed on the National Priorities List.Major cleanup work at Kress Creek began in 2005. EPA records describe the removal of contaminated soil and sediment from sections of Kress Creek and the West Branch of the DuPage River, followed by restoration of the affected areas. EPA's site profile says more than 129,000 cubic yards of contaminated material were removed during the cleanup. EPA's site profile dates the end of cleanup to October 2012, while the agency's September 3, 2026 release says cleanup was completed in 2014, with restoration continuing until 2025. An Illinois EPA page concerning the proposed deletion also gives October 2012 as the completion date.The cleanup was carried out section by section. Crews removed contaminated material from each area and then restored the affected sections with clean backfill and vegetation. Restoration work continued as the project progressed and remained underway after the cleanup phase, ultimately continuing through 2025. EPA and local officials marked the site's recent delisting at an event at McDowell Grove on September 3, 2026.The Kress Creek site was one of four National Priorities List sites created to address radioactive contamination associated with the former Rare Earths Facility. EPA says the Reed-Keppler Park site was deleted from the National Priorities List in 2010, followed by the Sewage Treatment Plant site in 2013. Kress Creek became the third of the four sites to be deleted.The Residential Areas site has also undergone cleanup but remains on the National Priorities List until the former Rare Earths Facility is addressed under the oversight of the Illinois Emergency Management Agency. The broader cleanup has therefore taken place in stages rather than as a single project. The Kress Creek delisting represents the completion of the Superfund process for that particular waterway and its associated contaminated areas.Removal from the National Priorities List does not necessarily mean that every trace of historical contamination has disappeared from an area. Rather, deletion indicates that EPA has determined that the site no longer requires further Superfund response action based on the cleanup completed there. EPA proposed removing Kress Creek from the National Priorities List in March 2026 and formally deleted the site in August. EPA and local officials subsequently held the September 3 event in DuPage County to mark the recent delisting.The Illinois Department of Natural Resources, which discusses Kress Creek as part of the state's natural resource trustee work, says the original source of the radioactive contamination has been addressed so that additional thorium is no longer entering the environment from the former facility. For communities around West Chicago and DuPage County, the delisting represents the latest stage in a cleanup that has stretched across decades. Contaminated material was removed from the creek and river system, affected areas were restored, and the federal government has now formally taken Kress Creek off the National Priorities List. The history of the site nevertheless illustrates how contamination from an industrial operation can persist long after the facility itself has stopped operating. The former Rare Earths Facility closed decades ago, but its radioactive legacy required years of investigation, excavation, disposal and restoration before the Kress Creek Superfund site could reach its 2026 delisting.
Article Summary: The US Environmental Protection Agency deleted the Kerr-McGee Kress Creek/West Branch DuPage River Superfund site in August 2026. The site no longer requires further Superfund response action to protect human health and the environment. The contamination was linked to the former Rare Earths Facility in West Chicago, which operated from 1932 to 1973.

Article Title: ShinyHunters hacker in FBI data theft held in Jordan
Article Text:
FBI declined to comment on any specific arrest or activity abroad but said that the bureau 'continues to aggressively probe the recent cyber incident allegedly involving ShinyHunters, having already worked with partners to arrest multiple subjects — and we will spare no resource in bringing each of the responsible individuals to justice.'

A suspected member of ShinyHunters hacking group, which says it stole data on every FBI employee, was detained in Jordan this week and is cooperating with FBI, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters.Saif al-Din Khader was detained by Jordanian authorities, the three sources said. Two of them said he was brought into custody on Tuesday. Reuters could not immediately determine the circumstances of Khader’s detention or where he is being held. Two sources said that he is helping FBI and global law enforcement locate the other hackers.FBI declined to comment on any specific arrest or activity abroad but said that the bureau “continues to aggressively probe the recent cyber incident allegedly involving ShinyHunters, having already worked with partners to arrest multiple subjects — and we will spare no resource in bringing each of the responsible individuals to justice.” Attempts to reach Khader and members of his family over the past week and a half have been unsuccessful.The detention of Khader — whose alleged hacker nickname is Rey — is the latest twist in the case of ShinyHunters. The prolific cyber extortion group, which has a long history of targeting major corporations around the world, is believed by experts to consist mainly of young, English-speaking hackers focused on data theft and extortion.
Article Summary: Saif al-Din Khader was detained by Jordanian authorities, the three sources said. Two of them said he was brought into custody on Tuesday. Two sources said that he is helping FBI and global law enforcement locate the other hackers. FBI declined to comment on any specific arrest or activity abroad.

US President Donald Trump said that his administration would soon send checks of “nearly $100” to more than 20 million older Americans to “help pay for their Medicare Part B premiums. ” Medicare Part B covers doctor visits, outpatient treatment and preventative tests.President, who made the announcement on Truth Social late Friday, said the money would come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, established in 2008 to enhance the original Medicare health insurance programme.The US midterm elections are barely a month away, and Trump’s Republican Party faces robust challenges from Democrats for its narrow control of the House and Senate.
